title: Why Do We Get Brain Freezes? The Science Explained
description: Ever wondered what causes that sudden, stabbing headache after eating ice cream too fast? Discover the fascinating science behind brain freezes.

sections.heading: What Actually Is a Brain Freeze?
paragraphs: We have all been there: you are enjoying a delicious scoop of ice cream on a hot summer day, you take one bite too many, and suddenly a sharp, intense ache hits the front of your head. Clinically known as sphenopalatine ganglioneuralgia, a brain freeze is a form of short-lived headache triggered by consuming something extremely cold.

Despite the dramatic name, nothing is actually freezing inside your head. Instead, it is a rapid physiological alarm system activated when the sensitive tissues in your mouth and throat experience a sudden drop in temperature. The good news is that these headaches are completely harmless and typically vanish within a minute or two.

sections.heading: The Anatomy of a Chilly Reflex
paragraphs: To understand why a brain freeze happens, we have to look at how your body regulates temperature. Your mouth and the roof of your palate are packed with blood vessels and nerves. When a large amount of ice-cold food or drink touches this area, it causes these blood vessels to rapidly constrict (narrow) and then quickly dilate (expand) as they try to warm back up.

This rapid change is detected by the trigeminal nerve, a major facial nerve responsible for sending sensation from your face, mouth, and sinuses to your brain. Because the trigeminal nerve also handles sensory input from the forehead, your brain gets slightly confused by the rapid-fire signals and misinterprets the cold sensation in the mouth as severe pain coming from the forehead.

sections.heading: Why Does Your Body Do This?
paragraphs: It might seem like your body is overreacting to a harmless treat, but this reflex actually serves a protective evolutionary purpose. The brain is arguably the most vital organ in the human body, and it relies on a relatively constant temperature to function properly.

When extremely cold substances enter the mouth near the base of the brain, the trigeminal nerve triggers a sudden pain response to make you stop consuming the cold item immediately. Essentially, a brain freeze is your body's way of shouting, 'Slow down! You are cooling down the control center too quickly!'

sections.heading: How to Prevent and Cure a Brain Freeze Fast
paragraphs: The absolute best way to avoid a brain freeze is simple: eat your ice cream, slushies, and frozen yogurt more slowly. Give your mouth time to adjust to the temperature rather than exposing the roof of your mouth to a massive wall of frozen mass all at once.

If you do happen to trigger a brain freeze, you do not have to just sit there and suffer. You can help warm the roof of your mouth back up quickly by pressing your tongue flat against it, or by drinking a glass of warm (not hot) water. Breaking the cycle of constriction and dilation stops the pain signals in their tracks.

faq.q: Can everyone get a brain freeze?
faq.a: Most people are capable of experiencing a brain freeze, though individuals who suffer from migraines may be more susceptible to them.

faq.q: How long does a brain freeze typically last?
faq.a: Most brain freezes are remarkably short-lived, usually peaking within seconds and completely disappearing in less than a minute or two.
No, brain freezes are entirely harmless physiological responses and cause no long-term damage to your brain or nerves.
